patient.chief_complaint: Confusion, ataxia, and eye movement abnormalities in a patient with NASH cirrhosis and celiac disease
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. P. is a 49-year-old woman with NASH cirrhosis, celiac disease, and hypothyroidism who presents after 7 days of severe vomiting and poor oral intake from a gastrointestinal illness. She is brought by a friend who found her ataxic, confused, and unable to walk. On exam, she has ophthalmoparesis (limited upward gaze and bilateral abduction), nystagmus on lateral gaze, truncal and appendicular ataxia, absent lower extremity reflexes, decreased vibration sensation in feet, and confusion with asterixis on prolonged arm extension. Her ammonia is 68 µmol/L — mildly elevated. She has a prior HE episode (NASH cirrhosis, MELD 13) and a recent history of 7 days of vomiting and poor intake on a background of celiac disease.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Concurrent Wernicke encephalopathy and hepatic encephalopathy in NASH cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 13) with celiac disease — thiamine 24 nmol/L from 7 days of vomiting and chronic malabsorption; ophthalmoparesis, nystagmus, ataxia mandate Wernicke treatment regardless of MRI.

differential.key_features: Ophthalmoparesis + nystagmus + ataxia + thiamine 24 nmol/L = Wernicke; MRI may confirm but does not exclude when absent.

differential.diagnosis: Celiac-related neurological syndrome (gluten ataxia, peripheral neuropathy)
differential.key_features: Acute onset less typical; treat celiac with strict gluten-free diet regardless.

optimal_actions.action: Send targeted laboratory studies: CBC, CMP, ammonia, magnesium, lactate, coagulation, B12, folate, thiamine_B1. Confirms liver dysfunction and screens for precipitants.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ammonia (mildly elevated); thiamine 24 nmol/L; cirrhosis features; celiac serologies; B12, folate.

optimal_actions.action: Non-contrast CT head — exclude structural alternate cause of AMS (hemorrhage, large stroke, mass) before any LP.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline; MRI is the key imaging.

optimal_actions.action: MRI brain with and without gadolinium — exclude alternate causes of AMS (acute ischemia, mass, Wernicke periaqueductal/mammillary changes, leptomeningeal disease) when CT is non-diagnostic or specific alternate diagnoses are suspected.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MRI brain — periaqueductal gray and mammillary body T2/FLAIR signal confirms Wernicke; absence does NOT exclude.

optimal_actions.action: Literature/guideline search to confirm West Haven grading, precipitant management, and lactulose/rifaximin dosing (Wernicke encephalopathy diagnosis and high-dose IV thiamine dosing; celiac neurologic manifestations; AASLD HE).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AASLD/EASL 2014 guidance retrieved; West Haven criteria and precipitant-driven management framework confirmed.

optimal_actions.action: Drug-interaction and medication-reconciliation review covering lactulose, rifaximin; high-dose parenteral thiamine; treat any vomiting with non-sedating antiemetics avoiding metoclopramide if extrapyramidal concern; flag any CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antiemetics, antihistamines) and confirm lactulose/rifaximin dosing in liver disease.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sedating/CNS-depressant medications identified; lactulose and rifaximin reviewed for hepatic dose adjustment.

optimal_actions.action: Consult neurology + hepatology + gastroenterology for celiac — coordinate definitive care, transplant candidacy assessment where applicable.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hepatology / critical-care guidance integrated into management.

optimal_actions.action: EEG — characterize encephalopathy and exclude NCSE. Triphasic waves are classic but non-specific (metabolic encephalopathies broadly); main role is exclusion of non-convulsive status epilepticus where the differential supports it.
Draw two sets of blood cultures, aerobic and anaerobic, before the first antimicrobial dose
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Growth identifies the organism and its susceptibility; a negative or pending culture does not exclude the diagnosis, and yield falls once treatment has started

optimal_actions.action: Send urine for microscopy and culture as part of the infection screen
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Pyuria and bacteriuria identify a urinary source; a negative result removes it from the list of precipitants

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

sequence_constraints.reason: In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect / hemorrhage on imaging before LP to avoid herniation risk.
In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect on neuroimaging before LP to avoid herniation risk.

critical_actions: High-dose IV thiamine 500 mg TID for 3 days then 250 mg IV daily for 5 days BEFORE any dextrose (Wernicke treatment dose, not prophylaxis).
Lactulose 30 mL TID; rifaximin 550 mg BID for HE.
Strict gluten-free diet; nutrition consult for celiac + cirrhosis.
Address vomiting (ondansetron preferred; avoid metoclopramide if possible).
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
Do not give dextrose before parenteral thiamine.
Do not under-dose thiamine — oral or IM are insufficient for active Wernicke; IV at 500 mg TID is the active-treatment regimen.
key_reasoning_points: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Ophthalmoparesis and nystagmus are NEVER features of HE — they point to Wernicke; treat both concurrently.
Wernicke is a clinical diagnosis; MRI is supportive but normal MRI does NOT exclude Wernicke.
Non-alcoholic Wernicke is well-described in celiac disease, hyperemesis, bariatric surgery, and chronic malabsorption.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the issue to celiac flare alone.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Celiac contributed via malabsorption-driven thiamine deficiency, but the immediate diagnoses are Wernicke + HE.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Ophthalmoparesis and nystagmus mandate Wernicke treatment even when cirrhosis 'explains' the confusion.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: concurrent Wernicke encephalopathy (non-alcoholic, from celiac malabsorption + vomiting) and HE; ophthalmoparesis/nystagmus are Wernicke signs incompatible with HE; hypomagnesemia blocks thiamine; MRI confirms periaqueductal + mammillary body signal
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools including MRI; two simultaneous diagnoses (Wernicke + HE) both requiring active treatment; non-alcoholic Wernicke is easy to miss.
